AESTHETICS · IDENTITY · LETTING GO

What Are We

Aesthetics （審美） · Identity
and the Art of Letting Go
I believe we all organize our homes from time to time, but after a while, things get messy again. I want to revisit Danshari so I can make clearer decisions about what to let go of and what to keep. Today, let's review it together.
MORE THAN OBJECTS

What do our things
mean to us?

THREE WAYS WE GET ATTACHED

Why letting go
feels difficult.

01
Endowment Effect [ɪnˈdaʊmənt ɪˈfɛkt]
稟賦效應

We may value something more simply because it belongs to us.

A cup used for ten years may feel worth more to you than the same cup in a store.
02
Sunk Cost Fallacy [sʌŋk kɔst ˈfæləsi]
沉沒成本謬誤

We let money already spent affect our choices, even though we cannot get it back.

An expensive jacket stays in your closet, even if you never wear it.
03
Loss Aversion [lɔs əˈvɝʒən]
損失趨避

Losing something can feel worse than gaining something of equal value.

You fear throwing away one useful object more than you enjoy the extra space.
A FAMILIAR STORY

The jacket
you never wear.

You bought an expensive jacket and wore it only once. You don't love it anymore, but every time you try to let it go, you remember how much you paid.

Are you keeping the jacket—or avoiding the feeling of wasted money?

THREE MORE IDEAS

Our things.
Our stories.

04
Extended Self [ɪkˈstɛndɪd sɛlf]
延伸自我

Objects can become part of our identity and personal story.

An old award reminds you of who you used to be.
05
Just-in-Case Thinking [ˌdʒʌst ɪn ˈkes ˈθɪŋkɪŋ]
萬一心態

We keep things because we imagine needing them in the future.

A spare blanket feels reassuring, even if no guest uses it.
06
Decision Fatigue [dɪˈsɪʒən fəˈtiɡ]
決策疲勞

Making many choices in a row can feel mentally tiring.

Sorting an entire room at once can become overwhelming.

A GENTLER WAY TO START

Slow
Decluttering.

Small changes are easier to live with than a perfect clean-up that lasts one day.

15
MINUTES

Start with one small area. Stop before it feels overwhelming.

?
MAYBE BOX

Put uncertain items aside. Give yourself time to decide.

1:1
ONE IN · ONE OUT

When a new item comes in, consider letting an old one go.
